strengths: The reported closed-loop results are strong: VADv2 achieves a driving score of 85.1 on Town05 Long, versus 76.1 for the strongest listed baseline, and 89.7 on Town05 Short. These results use camera-only perception and evaluate a town excluded from training.

The architecture offers a coherent integration of vectorized scene representations, trajectory-conditioned scoring, and scene-conflict supervision. Scoring multiple candidate trajectories is a practical approach to avoiding the averaging of incompatible driving behaviors.

The paper includes component ablations and qualitative examples of multiple plausible trajectories. Removing agent or map tokens degrades open-loop performance, supporting the usefulness of these representations.
weaknesses: The central probabilistic formulation is insufficiently specified. Equation 1 outputs an MLP value without defining positivity or normalization, and the paper does not distinguish a continuous probability density from categorical probabilities over the vocabulary. Section 3.3 does not define the target distribution, distance-dependent negative weights, or conflict-loss formula. If the target is one-hot, the stated KL divergence reduces to negative log-likelihood of the positive action; the separately described weighting of negative actions requires additional specification.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed contribution. There is no comparison against a deterministic regression head, a standard trajectory-vocabulary classifier, or a multimodal probabilistic baseline using the same encoder, training data, and wrapper. Removing distribution supervision entirely is not a meaningful substitute. Consequently, the improvements cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed probabilistic field rather than data scale, architecture, or auxiliary supervision.

Evidence for learning uncertainty is weak. The training demonstrations come from CARLA's official autonomous agent rather than diverse human drivers, and there are no quantitative measurements of calibration, likelihood, mode coverage, or behavior in ambiguous scenarios. Inference selects the highest-probability action, which is deterministic argmax selection despite repeated descriptions of sampling. Qualitative trajectory diversity alone does not establish a faithful behavioral distribution or justify using probabilities as confidence estimates.

The closed-loop comparisons leave important confounds unresolved. The paper uses approximately three million training frames but does not establish comparable training resources across baselines. Benchmark results include an unspecified rule-based wrapper, while the prominent claim of stable driving without that wrapper has no quantitative evaluation. Simulator version, weather and traffic settings, repeated runs, and uncertainty estimates are not sufficiently documented.

The ablations use only open-loop metrics, although the main contribution concerns closed-loop driving. Several reported effects are very small: removing conflict loss changes 3-second L2 from 0.290 to 0.291 meters and leaves 3-second collision rate unchanged at 0.039%. Without repeated trials or closed-loop ablations, the claimed importance of this loss is not convincing. Vocabulary size, trajectory coverage, positional encoding, and generalization to newly added candidates are also untested.

Novelty is overstated and insufficiently positioned. The approach closely resembles trajectory-set classification and learned candidate scoring, but the paper does not clearly establish its distinction from these approaches, including the cited CoverNet and MultiPath representations. The claim that deterministic planning cannot handle non-convex feasible spaces is too broad; averaging is a failure mode of particular regression objectives, not an inherent limitation of every deterministic policy.

Reproducibility and practical applicability remain limited. Essential architecture dimensions, optimization settings, training schedules, trajectory-sampling details, PID and wrapper parameters, and inference latency are absent. Evaluation is confined to two benchmarks within one simulated town, providing limited evidence for broader generalization or reliable real-time operation.

The training objective cannot be reproduced from Section 3.3. The construction of p_data, distance-dependent negative weights, and exact conflict loss are unspecified. Adding the demonstrated trajectory as the sole positive and treating alternatives as negatives does not, by itself, demonstrate recovery of the distribution of valid behaviors. The relationship between these weighted penalties and the stated KL-divergence objective needs clarification.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed contribution. There is no matched regression baseline using the same architecture, training data, supervision, and wrapper; no comparison against a straightforward trajectory-vocabulary classifier or mixture model; and no vocabulary-size or positional-encoding ablation. Removing the distribution loss removes expert-action supervision altogether, so that ablation does not establish an advantage over deterministic planning.

The claim of stable driving without a rule-based wrapper lacks quantitative support. Section 4.2 states that benchmark results use a wrapper, but its implementation and contribution are not reported. Closed-loop results with and without it are necessary to determine how much of the safety performance comes from the learned planner.

The evaluation does not directly validate uncertainty modeling. There are no likelihood, calibration, mode-coverage, or uncertainty-based decision experiments. Section 3.4 selects the highest-probability action, which is deterministic argmax selection despite repeated descriptions of sampling. Figure 3 illustrates multiple candidates but does not establish that their probabilities represent behavioral uncertainty or useful confidence.

The empirical scope and reproducibility are insufficient for the strength of the claims. Both benchmarks use Town05, with only 10 long routes and 32 short routes, and no repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are reported. Baseline training-data and evaluation conditions are not established as comparable to the approximately three million training frames. Architecture specifications, optimization settings, controller parameters, and runtime are also missing. All component ablations use open-loop metrics, where some improvements are extremely small: removing conflict loss changes three-second L2 from 0.290 to 0.291 meters and leaves three-second collision unchanged.

Novelty and motivation are overstated. The paper does not adequately distinguish its trajectory-set scoring approach from established multimodal, candidate-based, and probabilistic methods, including related trajectory-set prediction work it cites. The assertion that deterministic planning cannot handle nonconvex feasible spaces is too broad: averaging under a regression loss is a particular failure mode, not a limitation of all deterministic planners. Similarly, a trajectory demonstrated in one state is not automatically dynamically feasible from every current ego state.

The experiments do not isolate the main contribution. Removing distribution supervision entirely, as in Table 3, does not establish that probabilistic planning is better than alternative supervised planners.

Closed-loop results with and without the wrapper are necessary to attribute the gains to the learned policy.

Novelty is insufficiently established relative to trajectory-set classification and multimodal prediction, including cited work such as CoverNet and MultiPath. Applying related ideas to ego planning may be useful, but the broad first-of-its-kind claim and the distinction between a continuous probability field and candidate scoring need stronger justification.

The uncertainty claims are not directly evaluated. Inference selects the highest-probability action, and there are no calibration, likelihood, mode-coverage, or uncertainty-sensitive decision-making experiments. Qualitative candidate trajectories do not establish that the probabilities capture human behavioral uncertainty, especially when demonstrations come from CARLA's official agent.

Evaluation and reproducibility remain limited: both benchmarks use Town05, no repeated-run uncertainty is reported, and baseline training-data and wrapper conditions are not controlled. The open-loop ablations also show almost no benefit from conflict loss at three seconds: L2 changes from 0.291 to 0.290 m and collision rate remains 0.039%, weakening claims about its importance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important planning problem: direct trajectory regression can average incompatible driving behaviors. Scoring complete trajectory candidates conditioned on vectorized scene features is a practical approach to preserving multiple alternatives.

Reported results are promising across several benchmarks: Town05 Long driving score improves to 85.1 versus 76.1 for the strongest listed baseline, Bench2Drive reaches 76.15, and NAVSIM/NAVSIMv2 reach 89.3 PDMS and 85.8 EPDMS using camera inputs.

The evaluation includes useful vocabulary-size, sampling-strategy, training-data, scene-token, and planning-head ablations. Table 12 provides particularly relevant evidence: replacing regression with the proposed planner improves closed-loop driving score from 74.6 to 85.1 despite similar open-loop errors.
weaknesses: The central probability formulation is mathematically inconsistent as written. Equation 3 uses independent sigmoid outputs without normalization over actions, so these outputs do not define the categorical distribution required by the KL divergence in Equation 4. With one-hot supervision, Equation 5 rewards the demonstrated action but does not suppress other non-conflicting actions; assigning high scores to all such actions can minimize this term without learning their relative frequencies. The description also conflates action frequencies across all frames with the desired scene-conditioned distribution. These issues require an explicit, corrected objective and confirmation of what the experiments implemented.

The conflict objective in Equation 6 is unbounded below: minimizing log p(a) for a conflicting action drives the loss toward negative infinity as its probability approaches zero. This is not a conventional bounded negative-label loss such as -log(1-p(a)). Together with the normalization issue, this creates substantial uncertainty about the soundness and reproducibility of the core training procedure.

The conceptual novelty is overstated. The implemented mechanism is trajectory-vocabulary construction followed by scene-conditioned candidate scoring, while the introduction broadly characterizes existing learning-based planning as deterministic despite discussing probabilistic diffusion and flow methods later. A controlled comparison against a conventional normalized trajectory classifier or candidate-ranking planner is needed to establish what the proposed 'probabilistic field' contributes beyond this established formulation.

The experiments do not substantiate the stronger uncertainty claims. Inference selects the highest-scoring action deterministically, and there are no calibration, likelihood, mode-coverage, or uncertainty-based fallback evaluations. Similar performance among the top five candidates does not establish distinct behavioral modes; those candidates could be near-duplicate trajectories. The claimed ability to evaluate newly added actions is also not directly tested.

Attribution and statistical reliability remain unclear. Section 4.2 states that CARLA evaluation uses a rule-based wrapper, but the manuscript emphasizes stable operation without one and provides no explicit wrapper ablation. The deterministic-head comparison changes the prediction architecture as well as the objective. Results lack repeated-run variability, and the training protocol for Bench2Drive and the data/pretraining alignment of NAVSIM comparisons are insufficiently specified.

Real-world safety conclusions exceed the supplied evidence. The private 3DGS evaluation contains only 337 eight-second scenarios, with insufficient detail about split independence, agent reactivity, collision-rate denominators, and deviation thresholds. Table 15 labels collision values as percentages, whereas Table 4 describes ratios, leaving their scale unclear. Physical-vehicle deployment is referred to supplementary material without quantitative intervention or safety results in the manuscript.

Important implementation and feasibility details are missing. The manuscript does not provide a usable code link, optimizer and training schedules, or complete inference and controller settings. Selecting trajectories from demonstrations does not guarantee feasibility from the current ego state, and endpoint-only vocabulary sampling can overlook trajectories with different intermediate paths or speed profiles. These limitations weaken the claimed continuous action-space coverage and kinematic guarantees.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of trajectory regression: averaging incompatible driving behaviors can produce unsafe plans. Scoring complete trajectory candidates conditioned on scene information is a practical approach.

The reported evaluation is broad and promising: Town05 Long driving score improves to 85.1 versus 76.1 for the strongest listed baseline, and results also lead the presented Bench2Drive, NAVSIM, and NAVSIMv2 comparisons.

Table 12 provides useful evidence beyond open-loop imitation accuracy: replacing regression with the proposed planner improves closed-loop driving score from 74.6 to 85.1 despite nearly identical open-loop errors. Vocabulary, data-scale, scene-token, and sampling-strategy ablations provide additional empirical support.
weaknesses: The probability formulation has a central mathematical inconsistency. Equation 3 uses independent sigmoid outputs, which do not define a normalized categorical distribution over trajectories. Equations 4–5 nevertheless treat these outputs as such a distribution. Without normalization or negative-label terms, the stated distribution loss does not enforce competition among candidates and permits all candidate scores to approach one. The actual implemented objective needs to be specified and reconciled with the equations.

The conflict objective in Equation 6 is unbounded below: minimizing log p(a) for a conflicting action drives its contribution toward negative infinity as p(a) approaches zero. This is not a conventional negative-label likelihood such as -log(1-p(a)) and can dominate the combined objective. Together with the normalization issue, this prevents confidence in the method as specified.

The supervision description conflates scene-conditioned learning with marginal action frequencies counted across all frames. Per-example one-hot categorical training could learn a conditional distribution, but the globally estimated target described in Section 3.3 does not establish that formulation. No calibration, likelihood, or behavioral mode-coverage evaluation validates the claimed uncertainty modeling; good performance of five ranked candidates does not establish meaningful diversity or calibrated probabilities.

The methodological novelty is insufficiently distinguished from trajectory-vocabulary classification and candidate-scoring planners. Coordinate embeddings, cross-attention, and classification form a plausible system, but calling the scoring network a continuous probabilistic field does not establish a normalized continuous density. Comparisons against a conventional softmax trajectory classifier using the same vocabulary, scene encoder, and supervision are needed to isolate the proposed contribution.

The evaluation does not adequately isolate the learned planner. The introduction claims stable operation without a rule-based wrapper, while Section 4.2 states that CARLA evaluation uses one; no explicit wrapper-on/off comparison substantiates the stronger claim. Training-data parity with baselines is also unclear given the three million CARLA clips and 2,000 hours of real-world demonstrations. Repeated-run uncertainty is absent, which particularly matters for smaller gains such as 89.3 versus 88.6 NAVSIM PDMS.

The real-world conclusions exceed the documented evidence. The 3DGS evaluation contains 337 eight-second reconstructed scenarios, with insufficient detail about train/test separation, agent reactions, collision aggregation, and deviation thresholds. It supports performance in reconstructed simulation, but does not by itself establish robust real-world interaction safety. Vehicle deployment is deferred to supplementary material without quantitative results in the supplied manuscript.

Reproducibility and feasibility claims need improvement. Optimizer settings, training schedules, benchmark-specific training protocols, controller and wrapper details, and an accessible code link are missing. Selecting trajectories from demonstrations does not guarantee their feasibility from the current ego state, and endpoint-only vocabulary sampling can overlook trajectories with different intermediate motion but similar endpoints.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: direct trajectory regression can average incompatible driving behaviors. Scoring complete trajectory candidates is a practical approach to avoiding this failure mode.
Reported performance is strong across multiple benchmarks: 85.1 driving score on Town05 Long, 76.15 on Bench2Drive, 89.3 PDMS on NAVSIM, and 85.8 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2, using camera inputs.

The controlled comparison in Table 12 is particularly encouraging: probabilistic planning improves closed-loop driving score from 74.6 to 85.1 despite similar open-loop errors. Additional ablations examine vocabulary size, sampling strategy, training-data scale, and scene tokens.
The 3DGS evaluation extends the empirical scope beyond CARLA and reports reduced collisions against baselines sharing the same perception backbone.
weaknesses: The central probabilistic formulation is mathematically inconsistent as written. Equation 3 applies independent sigmoids without normalization, so its outputs need not form the categorical distribution required by Equations 4–5. With one-hot targets, Equation 5 also provides no penalty for high scores on unselected, nonconflicting actions. Furthermore, Equation 6 minimizes log p for conflicting actions and is unbounded below as their probabilities approach zero. These may be presentation errors, but the actual implemented objective must be established before the central method can be assessed as technically sound.

The novelty of the 'probabilistic field' is insufficiently distinguished from trajectory classification or candidate scoring using coordinate embeddings and cross-attention. The broad claim that existing planning methods are deterministic conflicts with the paper's own discussion of diffusion-based planners. A matched categorical trajectory-scoring baseline would help isolate the contribution beyond replacing regression with discretized action selection.

The experiments establish candidate quality more convincingly than uncertainty modeling. Similar performance among the top five candidates does not establish behavioral diversity, calibrated probabilities, or coverage of distinct feasible modes. Inference uses argmax selection, and no calibration, likelihood, uncertainty-based fallback, or out-of-vocabulary candidate evaluation supports the stronger distributional claims.

Evaluation comparability and reproducibility remain unclear. The paper uses three million CARLA clips and discusses 2,000 hours of proprietary driving data without clearly specifying training-data allocation for each benchmark or matching baseline training budgets. Bench2Drive training details, optimizer settings, training schedules, and repeated-run uncertainty are missing. The supplied manuscript also has an empty code-availability link.

Several safety and deployment claims exceed the evidence. Main CARLA results use a rule-based wrapper, but no quantitative wrapper-free comparison substantiates the claimed stability without it. The 3DGS evaluation contains only 337 eight-second scenarios, lacks confidence intervals and sufficient explanation of agent reactivity, and does not improve all deviation metrics. Real-vehicle deployment is referenced without quantitative results in the supplied manuscript.

Sampling a trajectory from demonstrations does not guarantee feasibility from the current ego state: initial speed, steering, and acceleration can differ from those of the source demonstration. Endpoint-only vocabulary sampling also need not preserve distinct intermediate paths or speed profiles. These limitations weaken the stated physical-feasibility and action-space-coverage guarantees.
